title: The Summit: the examiner's chair and ten climbs
summary: They sit five mixed peaks themselves, then administer them to their parents, grade the papers and explain every one at the whiteboard, and then climb the season summit: eight climbs over ground this season broke and two old friends from the earlier sprints.
materials: the field journal, open at the whole season's puzzle pages
five clean sheets, one peak each, so your parents sit a paper and not a screen
a red pen for marking, and the patience to use it kindly
the expedition wall map, for planting the last flag

steps.title: The summit, in order
steps.body:
Twelve weeks ago Python did not live on this laptop, the shop was one line on an idea page, and the far peaks on the wall map were only a poster.

Today Think runs in two parts, and in the first one you are not the candidate.

Part one is the family AMC. Five peaks sit on the next page, mixed topics, the way a real paper mixes them. Work all five yourself first, alone, with the page turned away from everybody. Then copy them onto five clean sheets, hand the paper to your parents, and let them sit it properly: no hints, no rescuing, nobody reading over a shoulder. Mark the papers with a red pen. Then stand at the whiteboard and explain every single peak, including the ones they got right, because a right answer for the wrong reason is the most interesting thing on any paper.

Before the season summit, there is one encore. Bring back the counting problem you invented in week 11: state it to the family, walk them through the cases you split it into, and show why your list of cases could never miss one or count one twice. A problem you can still teach months after you invented it is a problem you actually own.

Part two is the season summit: ten climbs. Eight of them are ground this season broke and no earlier summit has ever tested, and the last two are old friends, one from each earlier sprint, back on purpose. A thing you can still do three months later is a thing you own.

One rule holds all day, the same one Camp One and Camp Two ran on. This is not a test. A summit is a place you stand and look back at where you walked.

problems.prompt: Peak 1. A shape is drawn on grid paper. It starts as a rectangle 10 cm across and 8 cm tall, and then a rectangle 6 cm across and 5 cm tall is cut away from the top right corner, leaving an L. What is the area of the L, in square centimetres?
explanation: Draw the whole 10 by 8 rectangle first and forget the notch. That is 80 square centimetres.
The notch is a 6 by 5 rectangle, so 30 square centimetres were taken away.
80 less 30 leaves 50 square centimetres.
Check it the other way. A 10 by 3 strip is 30 and a 4 by 5 column is 20, the same 50.
problems.useAgain: when a shape is a rectangle with a bite taken out of it, or a few rectangles pushed together.
hints: The shape is not a rectangle, but it is hiding inside one. Draw the rectangle it would be if the notch were filled in.
Work out the area of that whole rectangle, then the area of the piece that was cut away.
problems.socraticHint: Is it easier here to add pieces up, or to start too big and take something away?

variant.prompt: A shape starts as a rectangle 12 cm across and 9 cm tall, and a rectangle 4 cm across and 3 cm tall is cut away from one corner. What is the area of what is left, in square centimetres?

problems.prompt: Peak 2. Nine people are standing at the stand, and every person shakes hands with every other person exactly once. How many handshakes happen altogether?
explanation: Look at it from one person first. That person shakes 8 hands, and there are 9 people, which looks like 72.
But every handshake was counted twice there, once from each side of it.
So halve the 72. There are 36 handshakes.
problems.useAgain: when every pair in a group has to be counted once, like handshakes, matches or lines between dots.
hints: Count from one person first. How many hands does one person shake?
Multiply that by the number of people, then ask whether any single handshake got counted more than once.
problems.socraticHint: When you and I shake hands, how many handshakes is that, and how many times did your method just record it?

variant.prompt: Seven teams each play every other team exactly once. How many games are played altogether?

problems.prompt: Peak 3. You have 7 different stickers and you are deciding which ones go on your notebook. You may use any of them, all of them, or none of them. How many different sticker collections are possible?
explanation: Take the stickers one at a time. Each is either on the notebook or off it.
Pair every collection with a row of seven yes or no marks, one mark per sticker.
Each collection makes one row and each row makes one collection, so the two piles are the same size.
Rows are easy: seven 2s multiplied together is 128, and the row of seven noes counts.
problems.useAgain: when a collection is too big to list and each thing in it is a separate yes or no choice.
hints: Do not try to list them. Ask what decision you make about one single sticker.
Write a collection as a row of yes or no marks, one mark per sticker, then count how many different rows there are.
problems.socraticHint: Is there a collection that a row of nothing but noes stands for, and does the question ask you to count it?

variant.prompt: A keychain can carry 9 different charms, and you may hang any of them, all of them, or none of them. How many different keychains are possible?

problems.prompt: Peak 4. A tag price of 20 dollars goes up by 10 percent on Friday. On Sunday the new price comes down by 10 percent. What does the tag say on Sunday?
explanation: The rise is 10 percent of 20 dollars, which is 2 dollars, so Friday's tag reads 22 dollars.
The fall is a tenth of the new price, not the old one, and a tenth of 22 dollars is 2.20.
So Sunday's tag is 22 less 2.20, which is 19.80 dollars.
Up ten and down ten does not come home. The fall was measured against a bigger number.
problems.useAgain: when a price changes twice by a percent, and each change is measured against whatever the price is at the time.
hints: A percent is always a percent of something. Ask what each of these two percents is measured against.
Work out Friday's price first, and take the second cut off that price rather than off the original tag.
problems.socraticHint: Are the two changes the same number of dollars, and if they are not, which one is bigger?

variant.prompt: A 40 dollar tag goes up by 25 percent, and then the new price comes down by 25 percent. What does the tag say at the end?

problems.prompt: Peak 5. How many four-digit whole numbers have at least one digit that is a zero?
explanation: Chasing the zeros means three places to watch, and a number like 1005 lands in two counts at once.
Count the opposite instead. Four-digit numbers run from 1000 to 9999, so there are 9000 of them.
A four-digit number with no zero has 9 choices for its first digit. The other three digits have 9 choices each, so 9 times 9 times 9 times 9 is 6561.
Take those away: 9000 less 6561 leaves 2439.
problems.useAgain: when the ones you want overlap in messy ways but the ones you do not want are easy to count.
hints: Numbers with a zero in the tens place and numbers with a zero in the ones place are not two separate piles. Some numbers sit in both.
Count how many four-digit numbers use no zero at all, digit by digit, and remember the first digit was never allowed to be zero anyway.
problems.socraticHint: Which is the shorter list to build here, the numbers you want or the numbers you do not want?

variant.prompt: How many four-digit whole numbers have at least one digit that is a 5?

steps.title: The examiner at the whiteboard
steps.prompt:
Mark the papers first, quietly, with no commentary. Then take the whiteboard and explain all five peaks, one at a time, in the order they were sat.

Record the sticker peak in full, because it is the one that argues rather than calculates. Do not open with the answer. Ask the room how they would start listing, let somebody get three or four collections written down, and only then hand them the row of yes and no marks. Show that every collection makes exactly one row and every row makes exactly one collection, so counting one pile has counted the other. Ask out loud whether the row of nothing but noes should count, and let somebody answer before you do.

For the other four, one rule holds: explain the mistake before you explain the answer. If nobody made a mistake on a peak, say what mistake the peak was built to catch and why it did not land.

Then say the last line out loud to the room. For one hour today the examiner's chair was yours, and it is the least frightening chair in the building.

problems.prompt: Climb 1, the shop's mirror. Suppose one unit sells for 4.00 dollars and cost 2.60 dollars to make. What is the profit on that sale as a percent of the price?
explanation: Find the profit first: 4.00 in, 2.60 of cost out, so 1.40 dollars is left.
Margin compares that profit with the price, not the cost, so it is 1.40 out of 4.00.
One percent of 4.00 dollars is 4 cents, and 1.40 is thirty five of those, so the margin is 35 percent.
Comparing profit with cost gives a bigger number. The words to watch are of the price.
problems.useAgain: when two shops of very different sizes have to be judged on the same scale.
hints: Two different numbers could sit underneath the profit here. The question names one of them.
Work the profit out in dollars first, then write it as a fraction of the price and turn that into hundredths.
problems.socraticHint: If a supermarket and your stand both made a dollar on one sale, would that alone tell you which one did better?

variant.prompt: One unit sells for 5.00 dollars and cost 3.00 dollars to make. What is the profit as a percent of the price?

problems.prompt: Climb 2, the bank. Suppose you leave 40 dollars in the family bank for 3 years, and it pays simple interest of 5 percent of the original 40 dollars every year. How much money is there at the end?
explanation: Simple interest is worked out on the money you put in, and only on that, every single year.
Five percent of 40 dollars is 2 dollars, so each year adds 2 dollars.
Three years add 6 dollars, so the pile is 46.00 dollars.
The snowball kind would pay on the growing pile instead, and would end a little higher.
problems.useAgain: when interest is paid on the starting amount every year rather than on the growing pile.
hints: Simple interest and the snowball kind are different animals. Which number does this one take its percent of, every single year?
Work out one year's interest first, then decide what several years does to it.
problems.socraticHint: Does the second year's interest know that the first year's interest arrived?

variant.prompt: You leave 60 dollars in the family bank for 4 years, at simple interest of 10 percent of the original 60 dollars every year. How much is there at the end?

problems.prompt: Climb 3, the angles. In triangle ABC the angle at A is 40 degrees and the angle at B is 65 degrees. The side BC is extended past C to a point D. How many degrees is angle ACD?
explanation: The three angles inside a triangle hold 180 degrees, so the angle at C is 180 less 40 less 65, or 75 degrees.
B, C and D sit on one straight line, and a straight line holds 180 degrees.
So angle ACD is 180 less 75, which is 105 degrees.
Shortcut worth keeping: the outside angle is the two far angles added, and 40 with 65 agrees.
problems.useAgain: when a side of a triangle is extended and the angle sitting outside it has to be found.
hints: Two straight-line facts are in play here, one about the triangle and one about the extended side.
Find the angle at C inside the triangle first, then use the straight line through B, C and D.
problems.socraticHint: How much of the straight line at C is already used up by the angle inside the triangle?

variant.prompt: In triangle PQR the angle at P is 30 degrees and the angle at Q is 85 degrees. The side QR is extended past R to a point S. How many degrees is angle PRS?

problems.prompt: Climb 4, the right angle. A right-angled triangle has its two short sides 12 cm and 16 cm long. How long is the longest side, in centimetres?
explanation: On a right-angled triangle the squares on the two short sides exactly fill the square on the longest.
Twelve squared is 144, sixteen squared is 256, and together they make 400.
So the square on the longest side is 400, and the side is the number that makes 400 by itself.
That is 20 centimetres. It came out whole because these sides are the 3, 4, 5 triple with every side times four.
problems.useAgain: when a right-angled triangle hands you two sides and asks for the third.
hints: The longest side is the one opposite the right angle. Square the two sides you were given before you do anything else.
Add those two squares together, then ask which number multiplied by itself gives that total.
problems.socraticHint: Will the answer be bigger or smaller than the longer of the two sides you were handed, and how do you know that before calculating?

variant.prompt: A right-angled triangle has its two short sides 5 cm and 12 cm long. How long is the longest side, in centimetres?

problems.prompt: Climb 5, the exponent in reverse. What is 4 to the power of negative 2, written as a fraction?
explanation: Going up one power multiplies by 4, so going down one power divides by 4.
Walk down from 4 squared, which is 16: then 4, then 1 at the zero power.
Two more steps down quarters it twice: one quarter, then one sixteenth.
So the answer is 1/16. A negative exponent on a counting number makes a small answer, not a negative one.
problems.useAgain: when an exponent is negative and you need the plain fraction it stands for.
hints: A negative exponent does not put a minus sign on the answer. It means you kept walking downwards past the zero power.
Write the powers of 4 downwards, starting from one you already know, and watch what every step does to the number.
problems.socraticHint: What does one step down the powers of 4 do to the number, and is there any reason that rule should stop at the zero power?

variant.prompt: What is 6 to the power of negative 3, written as a fraction?

problems.prompt: Climb 6, roots. The square root of 150 sits between two whole numbers that are next to each other. What is the smaller of those two whole numbers?
explanation: A square root asks which number, multiplied by itself, made this one.
So try the squares you know. Twelve times twelve is 144, thirteen times thirteen is 169.
150 sits between 144 and 169, so its root sits between the numbers that made them.
So the smaller one is 12. The root sits nearer 12, because 150 is much nearer 144.
problems.useAgain: when a square root is not a whole number and you only need to know which two whole numbers it lies between.
hints: You are not being asked for an exact answer here, so stop hunting for one.
List the squares of the whole numbers on either side until 150 is caught between two of them.
problems.socraticHint: Which whole numbers do you already know the squares of, and where does 150 land among them?

variant.prompt: The square root of 175 sits between two whole numbers that are next to each other. What is the smaller one?

problems.prompt: Climb 7, words into an equation. Suppose you sold twice as many small units as large ones. A small unit sells for 3 dollars and a large one for 8 dollars, and the day took in 42 dollars altogether. How many large units were sold?
explanation: Name what you do not know. Let L be the number of large units.
Twice as many small ones means 2L of them, and at 3 dollars each they take in 6L.
The large ones take in 8L, so the whole day is 6L plus 8L, which gathers to 14L, and that is 42.
So 14L is 42 and L is 3. Check: six small at 3 is 18, three large at 8 is 24.
problems.useAgain: when a word problem ties two unknown counts together and only one of them needs a letter.
hints: There are two unknown counts, but they are tied together. Which one should get the letter so the other can be written using it?
Write what the small units take in and what the large ones take in, both in the same letter, then say what the two add up to.
problems.socraticHint: Which of the two counts can you not write down at all until you know the other one?

variant.prompt: You sold three times as many small units as large ones. A small unit sells for 2 dollars and a large one for 5 dollars, and the day took in 44 dollars. How many large units were sold?

problems.prompt: Climb 8, reading the line. Suppose a price and profit table is plotted as points, with units sold across the bottom and profit up the side. The points sit at (0, -18), (3, -9), (6, 0) and (9, 9), and they all lie on one straight line. What is the profit at 12 units?
explanation: Look at one step along. From 3 units to 6 units the profit climbs from -9 to 0.
Nine dollars across 3 units means each unit adds 3 dollars, and that steady step is what per means.
From 9 units to 12 units is three more units, so 9 more dollars on top of the 9 already there.
That makes 18.00 dollars. The line crosses zero at 6 units, which is break-even.
problems.useAgain: when points lie on a straight line and you need to know what one step across is worth.
hints: Every step across of three units moves the point up by the same amount. Find that amount before anything else.
Work out how much profit one extra unit adds, then count how many units past the last plotted point you have to walk.
problems.socraticHint: What does one step to the right along this line do to the profit, and why is that the same thing as the word per?

variant.prompt: Points at (0, -20), (2, -12), (4, -4) and (6, 4) all lie on one straight line, with units sold across the bottom and profit up the side. What is the profit at 10 units?

problems.prompt: Climb 9, an old friend from sprint 1. A drawer holds socks in 4 colours, lots of every colour, and the room is dark. How many socks must you pull out to be sure of three that match?
explanation: Ask what the unluckiest hand looks like, not the luckiest.
The unluckiest is two of every colour: 4 times 2 is 8 socks, with no three matching yet.
The next sock is one of those colours, and every colour already holds two, so it makes three.
So 9 socks. Lots of every colour was there to stop you counting the drawer.
problems.useAgain: when a question asks how many to be sure, and the answer is the unluckiest case plus one more.
hints: Do not ask how lucky you could be. Ask how unlucky you could be and still have no three that match.
Fill every colour with as many socks as you can without ever making a match of three, then take one more.
problems.socraticHint: How many socks of one colour can you be holding before that colour stops being a way to fail?

variant.prompt: A drawer holds socks in 5 colours, lots of every colour, and the room is dark. How many socks must you pull out to be sure of four that match?

problems.prompt: Climb 10, a second old friend, from sprint 2. Suppose somebody claims that 13 is the largest prime there is. You multiply every prime up to 13 together and add one, giving 2 times 3 times 5 times 7 times 11 times 13, plus 1, which comes to 30031. What does that number show about the claim?
options: Nothing, because 30031 turns out not to be prime.
That 30031 is itself a prime, which is the only reason the claim fails.
That every prime up to 13 leaves one over in it, so it must have a prime factor bigger than 13.
That 13 really is the largest prime, since nothing at all divides 30031.
explanation: The part before the plus one is a multiple of every prime up to 13, so each leaves one over.
Every whole number above one is built out of primes, so 30031 has a prime factor.
That factor cannot be 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 or 13, so a bigger prime exists and the claim breaks.
The trap is thinking 30031 must be prime itself. It is 59 times 509 and still does the job.
problems.useAgain: when a claim that something is the largest of its kind has to be broken by building something bigger.
hints: You do not have to know whether 30031 is prime to answer this.
Divide it by each prime on the list in turn and watch what is left over every single time.
problems.socraticHint: If none of the primes on the list divide this number, what kind of number must be doing the dividing?

variant.prompt: Suppose somebody claims that 7 is the largest prime there is. You form 2 times 3 times 5 times 7, plus 1, which comes to 211. What does that show?
options: That no prime up to 7 divides 211, so a prime bigger than 7 has to exist.
Nothing, because 211 is bigger than every prime that was multiplied.
That 7 is still the largest prime, because 211 was built out of it.

steps.title: Write the marking page
steps.prompt:
Write the marking page for the family AMC: the page a stranger could grade from, having never met you or the problems.

One peak per block. Give the answer, then the shortest honest route to it, one idea per sentence. Then the line that matters most: what a person who got it wrong most likely did, in their words rather than yours. You have a real paper in front of you with real wrong answers on it, so use those instead of guessing.

Finish the page with two sentences of your own. First: of every peak this season put in the field journal, which one would you keep if you could keep only one, and why that one. Second: which of today's ten climbs felt like the newest ground under your feet, whether or not you got it right.

Then plant the last flag on the wall map.
